title: Decision-Irrelevant Is Not Learning-Irrelevant
content: Decision-focused learning encourages a model to retain what downstream decisions require, yet a learner may be trained on substantially more information than the deployed decision rule needs. We ask for the finite-sample decision effect of supervising information that is provably unnecessary for a fixed downstream decision family. Decision sufficiency alone cannot identify this effect. Under the same decision-preserving reduction and downstream family, we construct ordinary learning problems in which the additional supervision is exactly neutral, statistically beneficial, or statistically harmful. Exact neutrality holds when learning commutes with the reduction; away from commutation, shared latent information can improve estimation, whereas constrained shared capacity can displace decision-relevant structure. We derive a finite-sample separation for the harmful regime and an influence identity that traces nuisance supervision into deployed scores. Analytic controls reproduce all three signs. In a registered 810-configuration neural study, coupling-aware descriptors increase held-out-seed explanatory R² from 0.136 to 0.317. Two sequential Bayesian experimental-design case studies further exhibit different preferences among full, decision-reduced, and direct learners. The results separate deployment information requirements from the learning value of supervision.
